{{Short description|Analogy used to study vector fields}}
[[File:ChampSelonSigneDeDiv.pdf|thumb|300x300px|Three examples of vector fields. From left to right: a field with a source, a field with a sink, a field without either.]]

In the [[physical sciences]], [[engineering]] and [[mathematics]], '''sources and sinks''' (sometimes '''sources and drains''') is an analogy used to describe properties of [[vector field]]s. It generalizes the idea of fluid sources and sinks (like the [[Tap (valve)|faucet]] and [[Drain (plumbing)|drain]] of a bathtub) across different scientific disciplines. These terms describe points, regions, or entities where a vector field originates or terminates. This analogy is usually invoked when discussing the [[continuity equation]], the [[divergence]] of the field and the [[divergence theorem]]. The analogy sometimes includes '''swirls'''  and '''saddles''' for points that are neither of the two.

In the case of [[electric field]]s the idea of flow is replaced by [[field line]]s and the sources and sinks are [[electric charge]]s.

==Description and fluid dynamics analogy==
{{See also|Continuity equation|Divergence theorem}}
{{Multiple images
| image1            = Vektor5.svg
| image2            = Vektor3a.svg
| caption2          = A swirl
| caption1          = A saddle
| direction         = vertical
}}

In physics, a vector field  <math>\mathbf b(x,y,z)</math> is a function that returns a [[Vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]] and is defined for each point (with coordinates <math>x,y,z</math>) in a region of space. The idea of sources and sinks applies to <math>\mathbf b</math> if it follows a [[continuity equation]] of the form

:<math>\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot \mathbf b = s </math>,

where <math>t </math> is time, <math>a </math> is some quantity density associated to <math>\mathbf b</math>, and <math>s </math> is the source-sink term. The points in space where  <math>s>0 </math> are called a sources and when <math>s<0 </math> are called sinks. The integral version of the continuity equation is given by the [[divergence theorem]].

These concepts originate from sources and sinks in [[fluid dynamics]], where the flow is conserved per the continuity equation related to [[conservation of mass]], given by
:<math>\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot \mathbf v = Q </math>

where <math>\rho </math> is the [[Density|mass density]] of the fluid, <math>\mathbf v</math> is the [[flow velocity]] vector, and <math>Q </math> is the source-sink flow (fluid mass per unit volume per unit time). This equation implies that any emerging or disappearing amount of flow in a given volume must have a source or a sink, respectively. Sources represent locations where fluid is added to the region of space, and sinks represent points of removal of fluid. The term <math>Q </math> is positive for a source and negative for a sink.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Guyon |first=Etienne |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c9OjnsX4nNQC&dq=sources+and+sinks+in+hydrodynamics&pg=PA217 |title=Physical Hydrodynamics |date=2001-04-26 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-851745-0 |language=en}}</ref> Note that for [[incompressible flow]] or time-independent systems, <math>Q </math> is directly related to the divergence as

:<math>\nabla\cdot \mathbf v=Q </math>.
For this kind of flow, [[solenoidal vector field]]s (no divergence) have no source or sinks. When at a given point <math>Q=0 </math> but the curl  <math>\nabla\times \mathbf v \neq  0 </math>, the point is sometimes called a swirl.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Pandey |first=R. K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PjDn8u7F4rYC&dq=vector+field+sources+sinks+swirls&pg=PA115 |title=Vector Analysis |date=2007 |publisher=Discovery Publishing House |isbn=978-81-8356-297-3 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Aratyn |first1=Henrik |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JFmUQGd1I3IC&dq=vector+field+sources+and+sinks&pg=PA39 |title=A Short Course in Mathematical Methods with Maple |last2=Rasinariu |first2=Constantin |date=2006 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-256-461-0 |language=en}}</ref> And when both divergence and curl are zero, the point is sometimes called a saddle.<ref name=":0" />

== Other examples in physics ==

===Electromagnetism===
[[File:Electric-dipole-field-lines-and-equipotential-lines.svg|thumb|300x300px|Field lines of an [[Electric dipole moment|electric dipole]]. Field lines go from positive charge (source) to the negative charge (sink).]]
In [[electrodynamics]], the [[current density]] behaves similar to hydrodynamics as it also follows a continuity equation due to the [[charge conservation]]:
:<math>\frac{\partial \rho_e}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot \mathbf j = \sigma  </math>,

where this time <math>\rho_e </math> is the [[charge density]], <math>\mathbf j</math> is the [[current density]] vector, and <math>\sigma </math> is the current source-sink term. The current source and current sinks are where the current density emerges <math>\sigma>0 </math> or vanishes <math>\sigma<0 </math>, respectively (for example, the source and sink can represent the two poles of an [[electrical battery]] in a closed circuit).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Guru |first1=Bhag Singh |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qzNdDtZUPXMC&dq=current+density+source+and+sink+electromagnetism&pg=PA139 |title=Electromagnetic Field Theory Fundamentals |last2=Hiziroglu |first2=Hüseyin R. |date=2009-07-23 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-45192-5 |language=en}}</ref>

The concept is also used for the electromagnetic fields, where fluid flow is replaced by [[field line]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Snieder |first=Roel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=digNulgdDBIC&dq=sinks+and+sources+divergence&pg=PA69 |title=A Guided Tour of Mathematical Methods: For the Physical Sciences |date=2004-09-23 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-83492-6 |language=en}}</ref> For an [[electric field]] <math>\mathbf  E</math>, a source is a point where electric field lines emanate, such as a positive [[Electric charge|charge]] (<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf  E>0</math>), while a sink is where field lines converge (<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf  E<0</math>), such as a negative charge.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kelly |first=P. F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ampYBQAAQBAJ&dq=electric+field+source+sink+charges&pg=SA2-PA13 |title=Electricity and Magnetism |date=2014-12-01 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4822-0635-7 |language=en}}</ref> This happens because electric fields follow [[Gauss's law]] given by
:<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf  E=\rho_e/\epsilon_0</math>,
where  <math>\epsilon_0</math> is the [[vacuum permittivity]]. In this sense, for a [[magnetic field]] <math>\mathbf  B</math> there are no sources or sinks because there are no [[magnetic monopole]]s as described by [[Gauss's law for magnetism]] which states that 
:<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf  B=0</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Tinker |first1=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ecKdEAAAQBAJ&dq=there+are+no+sources+and+sinks+of+magnetic+field&pg=PA516 |title=Further Mathematics for the Physical Sciences |last2=Lambourne |first2=Robert |date=2000-06-08 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-471-86723-4 |language=en}}</ref> 
Electric and magnetic fields also carry energy as described by [[Poynting's theorem]], given by

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} +\nabla\cdot\mathbf{S}= -\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E} </math>

where <math>u </math> is the [[Energy density|electromagnetic energy density]], <math>\mathbf S </math> is the [[Poynting vector]] and <math>- \mathbf J\cdot \mathbf E </math> can be considered as an energy source-sink term.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zangwill |first=Andrew |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tEYSUegp9WYC&dq=current+density+source+and+sink+electromagnetism&pg=PA508 |title=Modern Electrodynamics |date=2013 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-89697-9 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Newtonian gravity ===
[[File:Earth-moon-field.svg|thumb|Gravitational field lines between Earth and the Moon. For gravity there are only sinks.]]


Similar to electric and magnetic fields, one can discuss the case of a Newtonian [[gravitational field]] <math>\mathbf  g</math> described by [[Gauss's law for gravity]],
:<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf  g=-4\pi G  \rho</math>,
where <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]]. As gravity is only attractive (<math>\rho\geq0</math>), there are only gravitational sinks but no sources. Sinks are represented by [[Point particle|point masses]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Campos |first=Luis Manuel Braga da Costa |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gwPLBQAAQBAJ&dq=gravitation+sinks+no+sources&pg=PA393 |title=Complex Analysis with Applications to Flows and Fields |date=2010-09-03 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4200-7120-7 |language=en}}</ref>

===Thermodynamics and transport===
In thermodynamics, the source and sinks correspond to two types of [[thermal reservoir]]s, where energy is supplied or extracted, such as [[heat flux]] sources or [[heat sink]]s. In [[thermal conduction]] this is described by the [[heat equation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2.2.5 Heat Sinks and Sources |url=https://www.iue.tuwien.ac.at/phd/holzer/node27.html |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=www.iue.tuwien.ac.at}}</ref> The terms are also used in [[non-equilibrium thermodynamics]] by introducing the idea of sources and sinks of [[Entropy|entropy flux]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Demirel |first1=Yasar |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sKh7DwAAQBAJ&dq=thermodynamics+divergence+heat+sink+and+source&pg=PA157 |title=Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics: Transport and Rate Processes in Physical, Chemical and Biological Systems |last2=Gerbaud |first2=Vincent |date=2018-11-24 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-444-64113-7 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Chaos theory ===
In [[chaos theory]] and [[complex system]], the idea of sources and sinks is used to describes  [[Attractor|repellors and attractors]], respectively.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qvZRAAAAMAAJ&dq=vector+field+sources+sinks+swirl+saddles&pg=PA832 |title=Image Understanding Workshop: Proceedings of a Workshop Held at Los Angeles, California, February 23-25, 1987 |date=1987 |publisher=Morgan Kaufmann Publishers |isbn=978-0-934613-36-1 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Murdock |first=James A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZPvtSjPf0_MC&dq=attractors+%22repellors%22+sources+sinks+saddles&pg=PA320 |title=Perturbations: Theory and Methods |date=1999-01-01 |publisher=SIAM |isbn=978-0-89871-443-2 |language=en}}</ref>

==In mathematics==

=== Complex functions ===
This terminology is also used in [[complex analysis]], as [[complex number]]s can be described as vectors in the [[complex plane]]. Sources and sinks are associated with [[zeros and poles]] of [[meromorphic function]]s, representing inflows and outflows in a [[harmonic function]]. A complex function is defined as a source or a sink if it has a pole of order one.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Brilleslyper |first1=Michael A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pib4DwAAQBAJ&dq=sources+and+sinks+complex+analysis+complex+zero+and+poles&pg=PA170 |title=Explorations in Complex Analysis |last2=Dorff |first2=Michael J. |last3=McDougall |first3=Jane M. |last4=Rolf |first4=James S. |last5=Schaubroeck |first5=Lisbeth E. |date=2012-12-31 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-88385-778-6 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Topology ===
In [[topology]], the terminology of sources and sinks is used when discussing a vector field over a compact [[differentiable manifold]]. In this context the [[index of a vector field]] is +1 if it is a source or a sink, if the value is -1 it is called a saddle point. This concept is useful to introduce the [[Poincaré–Hopf theorem]] and the [[hairy ball theorem]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Richeson |first=David S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kv2EDwAAQBAJ&dq=vector+field+sources+and+sinks+hairy+ball+theorem&pg=PA209 |title=Euler's Gem: The Polyhedron Formula and the Birth of Topology |date=2019-07-23 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-19199-7 |language=en}}</ref>

== Other uses ==
Other areas where this terminology is used include [[source–sink dynamics]] in [[ecology]] and [[current source density analysis]] in neuroscience, as well as in the A/V industry where installers refer to signal destinations, such as video projectors or video monitors as 'sinks.'<ref>https://avlatency.com/terminology/#sink-device</ref><ref>https://cie-group.com/how-to-av/videos-and-blogs/what-is-an-av-sink-device</ref>
